name: al-Malik al-Amjad
bio: Majd al-Din Abu al-Muzaffar Bahram Shah ibn Farrukhshah ibn Shahanshah ibn Ayyub, known as al-Malik al-Amjad, was an Ayyubid prince whom Saladin, his father's uncle, confirmed as lord of Baalbek when his father died in 578 AH (1182 CE); he held it for some forty-nine years, until his cousin al-Ashraf Musa besieged the town for about ten months and took it from him in 627 AH (1229–30 CE). The historian Ibn Wasil says he loved scholars and poets and rewarded them generously, and that “there was no better poet among the house of Ayyub”; al-Safadi, after quoting a few of his pieces, called them “middling verse”. He moved to Damascus, where he had locked up one of his slaves on suspicion of stealing an ornamented inkstand; the slave came out with a drawn sword and struck him down as he sat playing backgammon at the door, and he died on the night of 12 Shawwal 628 AH (August 1231 CE) and was buried in his father's tomb outside the city. His diwan survived in several manuscripts, the oldest copied in Damascus in 633 AH (1236 CE), and was edited by Nazim Rashid (Baghdad, 1983) and by Gharib Muhammad Ali Ahmad (Egypt, 1991).
